analysis.one_liner: Doubles the notice and back pay employers owe workers before plant closings and mass layoffs.
analysis.headline: The bill to extend layoff notice to 90 days and double employer penalties never got a hearing or vote in the Senate HELP Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FOREWARN Act would have amended the existing WARN Act, which requires employers to warn workers before shutting a plant or conducting a mass layoff. It would have stretched the required written notice from 60 days to 90, doubled the back pay an employer owes workers for every day of a violation, and lowered the size thresholds so smaller employers and smaller layoffs would be covered for the first time. It also would have let the Labor Department — or a state attorney general — sue on workers' behalf, ordered the Department to publish plain-language materials on worker rights, and required employers to report closings and layoffs to the Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at plants and large work sites facing a closing or mass layoff. They would get 90 days of warning and pay instead of 60, double back pay when employers skip the warning, and a Labor Department that can sue for them instead of leaving each worker to hire a lawyer. Smaller firms' employees — at employers with 50 or more workers — would gain WARN protection they do not have today. Communities and state agencies would also get earlier warning so they can line up retraining and aid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing plant closings and layoffs

how_it_helps.text: Workers at plants being closed or downsized would get 90 days of pay protection instead of 60, giving more time to find work before the paycheck stops.
Employers who skip the notice would owe double back pay for every day of violation for up to 90 days, a much stronger reason to actually warn workers.
The Labor Department, or a state attorney general if the Department sits on a case for six months, could sue on workers' behalf — so a laid-off machinist would no longer have to fund a lawsuit alone.

More workers would be covered at all: the employer-size threshold drops from 100 to 50 employees and the layoff-size triggers are cut in half, so layoffs at smaller factories would trigger the notice duty.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that close plants or conduct mass layoffs. They would owe up to 90 days of notice pay instead of 60, double back pay for violations, and new compliance and reporting duties — including firms with 50 to 99 employees that are currently exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers closing plants or laying off workers

drawbacks.text: The bill roughly doubles employer liability in a closing: 90 days of notice instead of 60, double back pay instead of single, and coverage extended to firms with as few as 50 employees — costs that land on the employer making the shutdown decision, including smaller employers newly covered.

A 90-day paid notice obligation gives employers an incentive to make closing or layoff decisions earlier and more cautiously, which could delay restructuring; some abrupt failures simply cannot support 90 days of payroll.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: workers suddenly losing a job get three months' pay protection instead of two, and a government enforcer makes the law mean something. The costs fall on the employers being closed or downsized, in extra payroll during the notice period and double damages when they fail to warn — which is the point of the law, but it is a genuine cost, and extending coverage down to 50-employee firms spreads compliance work to smaller businesses. For a law meant to give families time to plan around a lost paycheck, the design is straightforward and the cost side is the intended deterrent; the honest objection is that no notice period fully cushions an abrupt shutdown and that some marginal plants might close sooner rather than later.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on July 16, 2007, joined by Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; no further committee or floor action ever appears in the record.
Nine Democratic senators cosponsored; no Republican did.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: they keep the current rules of 60 days' notice, single back pay, higher coverage thresholds, and no government enforcer, so a closing costs them less in notice pay and penalties.

industries.industry: Employers conducting plant closings and mass layoffs (manufacturing and other large employers)
industries.note: The bill directly raises the cost of closing or downsizing: an extra month of paid notice, double back-pay liability, coverage extended to smaller firms, and a Labor Department that can sue. Its interest in cheaper, faster shutdowns runs against the workers' interest in notice and pay.
